approvalNote: Self-help tools from cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) (demo). The questions, thinking traps, example thoughts and exposure ladder templates are placeholder content: a clinical expert must review and approve them before real use. Rules decide how an exercise proceeds – AI may only phrase the questions and propose examples, which the client accepts or edits themselves.

tools.title: Exploring a thought
tools.description: Pause on a situation: what happened, what you thought and how it felt – and look for a more balanced way to see it.
tools.purpose: Helps you notice automatic thoughts and thinking traps and practise other ways of interpreting a situation.
tools.caution: If going through the situation makes the feeling unbearable, stop. You can stop at any time. This exercise does not replace help in a crisis.
tools.sourcePlaceholder: Source: [placeholder] – CBT thought diary, a self-help version approved by a professional.

tools.title: Behavioural experiment
tools.description: Test a frightening prediction with a small, safe experiment – and see what really happens.
tools.purpose: Helps you check predictions through experience instead of leaving them to avoidance.
tools.caution: Choose a small and safe experiment. The experiment does not have to succeed – every result is information.
tools.sourcePlaceholder: Source: [placeholder] – CBT behavioural experiment, a self-help version approved by a professional.

tools.title: Exposure ladder
tools.description: Build a ladder for a situation you avoid, from the easiest step to the hardest, and move up one step at a time at your own pace.
tools.purpose: Gradual practice helps anxiety ease in situations you have started to avoid.
tools.caution: Go at your own pace. Start with a step that makes you only a little nervous. If the anxiety becomes unbearable, stop and go back to an easier step. Exposure is not done in a crisis.
tools.sourcePlaceholder: Source: [placeholder] – graded exposure, a self-help version approved by a professional.

traps.label: Fortune telling
traps.description: I assume I know in advance that things will go badly.
patterns: \b(won ?'?t|will not|not going to|never going to) work( out)?\b
traps.alternative: I can't know in advance how it will go. I've prepared, and I can do well enough, even if I feel nervous.

traps.label: Mind reading
traps.description: I assume I know what other people think of me.
traps.alternative: I can't know what others are thinking. Most people focus on the topic – not on whether I'm nervous.

traps.label: Catastrophising
traps.description: I expect the worst possible outcome – and that I couldn't cope with it.
traps.alternative: Even if something went wrong, it would be unpleasant – but I would get through it.

traps.label: All-or-nothing thinking
traps.description: I see things as either perfect or a complete failure.
traps.alternative: It doesn't have to be perfect to be good enough.

traps.label: Should statements
traps.description: I make unreasonable demands of myself and criticise myself when I don't meet them.
traps.alternative: I want to do well, but I'm also allowed to feel nervous and to be a work in progress.

traps.label: Labelling
traps.description: I give myself a negative label on the basis of one situation.
traps.alternative: One difficult situation doesn't define me. I can do many things.

traps.label: Emotional reasoning
traps.description: I conclude from a feeling that something is true: because I feel scared, it must be dangerous.
traps.alternative: Feeling nervous tells me this matters to me – not that I will fail.

traps.label: Overgeneralising
traps.description: I conclude from one experience that it always happens this way.
traps.alternative: One time doesn't mean it will always happen this way.

traps.label: Discounting the positive
traps.description: I play down my successes and only pay attention to what went badly.
traps.alternative: My successes are just as real as my failures.

steps.question: How are you feeling today?
And how much anxiety or nervousness have you felt today?
Has any of these got worse?
Your therapist's follow-up question: {track} – how strong is it today?
Would you like to tell me what happened today?
steps.placeholder: For example, what affected your day…

thought_record.title: Exploring a thought
thought_record.intro: Good, let's do that. We'll take it slowly – you can skip questions or stop at any time.

steps.question: Tell me briefly which situation is on your mind – what happened, or what is coming up?
steps.placeholder: E.g. on Monday I have to give a presentation to the team

steps.question: When you think about the situation, what is the first thought that comes to mind?
What feelings does the thought bring up in you?
How strong is the feeling on a scale of 0–10 when you think about the situation?
What have you done – or what have you felt like doing?
steps.placeholder: E.g. I put off preparing and wondered whether I could cancel

steps.question: The mind easily takes familiar shortcuts, which are called thinking traps. Do you recognise any of these in your thought?
What makes the thought feel so true?
steps.placeholder: E.g. last time I was so nervous that my voice shook

steps.question: What if a good friend told you the same thought – what would you say to them?
steps.placeholder: E.g. you've prepared well, and your nervousness shows much less than you think

steps.question: How could you think about the situation in a slightly more balanced way?
When you read that new thought, how strong is the feeling now, 0–10?
What would you like to try next?

experiment.title: Behavioural experiment
experiment.intro: Let's do a small behavioural experiment: we'll write down your prediction, plan a safe experiment and later look at what really happened.

steps.question: What are you afraid will happen?
steps.placeholder: E.g. if I speak in a meeting, my voice will shake and everyone will notice

steps.minLabel: I don't believe it at all
steps.question: How strongly do you believe the prediction now, 0–10?
What small experiment could you use to test the prediction?
steps.placeholder: E.g. I'll make one comment in Tuesday's meeting

steps.question: When will you do the experiment?
What really happened when you did the experiment “{plan_short}”?
steps.placeholder: E.g. my voice shook for a moment, but nobody commented

steps.minLabel: I don't believe it at all
steps.question: How strongly do you believe the original prediction now, 0–10?
What did you learn from the experiment?
steps.placeholder: E.g. my nervousness doesn't show as much as I think

exposure.title: Exposure ladder
exposure.intro: Let's build an exposure ladder together. With it, you get used to the situation in small steps, from the easiest to the hardest – and you decide the pace.

steps.question: Which situation makes you most nervous – or what have you started to avoid?
steps.placeholder: E.g. giving a presentation to the team

steps.question: How much nervousness would it bring up now, 0–10?
Here is a suggested ladder, from the easiest step to the hardest. Edit the steps so that the ladder feels like your own.
A good start makes you only a little nervous. Which step would you like to start with?
When could you take the first step?
Step “{step_text}”: how much anxiety did you feel just before, 0–10?
And at its strongest?
And at the end, once you had done the step?
What did you notice?
steps.placeholder: E.g. the nervousness eased within a couple of minutes

steps.question: How shall we continue?
When will you do the next practice?

steps.text: Practise the start of the presentation out loud on your own
Record a two-minute presentation and watch the recording
Give the start of the presentation to one colleague you know well
Make one comment in a team meeting
Present one slide in a team meeting
Give the whole presentation to the team

experimentPlans: I'll make one comment in the next meeting and see whether anyone notices that I'm nervous.
After the presentation, I'll ask a colleague I trust how it sounded to them.

steps.text: Write down the most important points of the call in advance
Call someone you know and practise the same sentences
Make a short call, for example to check opening hours

experimentPlans: I'll make a short call and write down what actually happened.

steps.text: Greet a neighbour or colleague and ask how they are
Join the coffee break and listen to the conversation
Share one thing about yourself in a conversation
Go to the event and stay for at least an hour

experimentPlans: I'll share one thing about myself in a conversation and see how others react.

steps.text: Imagine the situation for a couple of minutes
Do a small, short version of the situation
Do the situation with someone you know

experimentPlans: I'll do a small version of the situation and write down what actually happened.

texts.stopped: All right, let's stop for now. The unfinished exercise was not saved. You can start again at any time.
texts.reask: You can answer by choosing an option below – or skip the question. You can also stop the exercise.
texts.thought_record_done: Great work! The entry was saved in your thought diary, and only you can see it unless you share it yourself.
texts.experiment_done: The experiment is planned. I'll remind you on the agreed day – then tell me what really happened.
texts.experiment_review_done: Thank you for testing your prediction. The result was saved in your exercises.
texts.exposure_done: Your ladder is ready! The first step is on your task list – go at your own pace.
texts.exposure_attempt_done: Thank you for taking the step. The practice was logged on your ladder.
texts.checkin_offer: It sounds like there was a lot of nervousness in your day. Would you like to look at the situation more closely?
texts.situation_offer: It's understandable that the coming situation already makes you nervous. In a situation like this, it can help to pause for a moment and look at your own thoughts. Would you like us to explore them together?
texts.avoidance_offer: It seems you've started to feel like avoiding the situation. That's understandable – avoiding brings relief for a moment. In the longer run, though, the fear can grow. Would you like us to build a ladder that helps you get used to the situation one step at a time?
texts.self_critical_offer: It sounds like you're being quite hard on yourself right now. A thought like that can weigh a lot. Would you like us to explore it together?
texts.task_due: Today is the agreed day: {title}. Tell me how it went once you've done it – you can also postpone the practice.
texts.homework_due: Your therapist's between-session task: {title}. You can do it here whenever it suits you.
